segments.title: The scenario and the test
sections: The Line You Couldn't Put A Stop Behind

cues.text: You know the moment. Price runs up into a line you drew, and the trade looks right.
Then you go to place the stop and there is nowhere to put it. Two ticks feels too tight. Twenty points feels arbitrary.
The problem was not the entry. It was the line.
Now, the test. It is called the stop-structure test, and it has two parts.
Part one: you can name something that already happened at that price. A session high. A volume cluster. A value edge.
Part two: you can name a price beyond it where the reason for the trade is gone. That is where the stop sits.
Pass both parts and it is a level. Fail either one and it is a line, however good it looks.
The example. Take the prior session's regular-session high, 24,186.50. Six five-minute bars traded up into it and turned, and nothing traded above it. Invented price, composite chart.
If you are short from that high and price trades through it and stays, the sellers who defended it are gone, and so is your reason for being short.
The test does not ask whether price reacted at a line, or how many times. Price reacts everywhere, in hindsight. Hindsight is undefeated. The test asks whether the structure gives your stop a job.
The rule: write one sentence. The stop goes behind this price because of what happened there. If you cannot fill both blanks from the chart, it is not a level.

Getting it wrong looks like a stop chosen after the entry, as a number of points that felt right. Be honest about the order: you picked where you wanted to trade first, and went looking for a reason second. The chart never got a vote.

check.q: Under the stop-structure test, what makes a price a level?
options: Price has reacted there more than once
You can name something that already happened there and a price beyond it at which the reason for the trade is gone
A widely watched indicator sits there
check.why: The test asks whether the structure gives your stop a job, not whether price has reacted. Price reacts everywhere in hindsight.

check.q: A moving average sits at 24,150. Why does it fail the test?
options: It moves more slowly than price
Nothing happened at that price, so there is no price beyond it at which you are wrong and no place for a stop
Moving averages are only used on daily charts
check.why: The line is there because of an arithmetic choice, and in ten minutes it will be somewhere else.

check.q: What is the one sentence a price must fill in to count as a level?
options: The stop goes behind [price] because [what happened there]
check.why: If you cannot fill both blanks from the chart, it isn't a level.

check.q: A row on your level list has a blank in its stop sentence. What happens to it?
options: It stays and you fill it in during the session
It moves to the target column
It is kept at half size
check.why: Every row carries the stop sentence, written before the session.

cues.text: Zones. Structure is never one price. A high is made by bars, a value edge sits beside rows of volume, a node has a top and a bottom.
So every level is written as a zone: a price band with two edges.
The far edge is the edge on the far side from where price arrives. For a level above price it is the top of the zone. For a level below, the bottom. The stop goes behind it.
The example. On the same high, the bar printed 24,186.50 and its body closed at 24,180.25. One construction runs the zone from 24,180.25 to 24,186.50, six and a quarter points.
Price arrives from underneath, so the near edge is 24,180.25 and the far edge is 24,186.50.
The zone's width is part of your risk, and where inside the zone you get filled decides how far the stop is. Module 14 turns both into numbers.
Choose a construction once per level type and keep it, so a level that failed can be told apart from a level that was drawn differently.

The rule: every level is a zone with a near edge and a far edge. Where two zones overlap, they become one zone, and it keeps every slug in it. A slug is the short name you log a level under, like pd-high for the prior-day high.

Getting it wrong is a single line with a stop two ticks beyond it. Or the classic: price trades through the zone, so you redraw the zone wider, and now the trade is fine again. It is not. The zone moved. The structure did not.

check.q: For a level above current price, which edge is the far edge?
check.why: The far edge is on the far side from where price arrives, and the stop goes behind it.

check.q: Price trades inside the zone 24,180.25 to 24,186.50 and never goes beyond 24,186.50. What is that?
check.why: Trading inside a zone is a test. Acceptance through the whole zone is what changes the read.

check.q: A zone is redrawn wider after price traded through it, so the trade "is still fine". What does that reveal?
options: The zone was built too tightly at first
The zone is being drawn to fit the trade you are in
The far edge was on the wrong side
check.why: The fix is one construction line per slug, with edges written by 09:25 and never moved during the session.

check.q: When are zone edges written, and can they move during the session?
options: At the open, and they follow price
By 09:25, and they are never moved during the session
After the first trigger, and they can be widened
At the close, and they carry over unchanged
check.why: Edges are written before the session and left alone.

segments.title: The two lists
sections: The Pre-Marked List And The 16:00 Boundary

cues.text: The list you mark before the session. It is fixed, and it is built from finished data. Six things go on it.
One: the prior day's high and low.
Two: the prior day's value edges and its volume point of control, the VPOC.
Three: settlement.
Four: the overnight high, low and point of control.
Five: the prior week's high and low.
Six: nodes from a multi-session volume profile.

Session scope. Each one has a session scope: the bars that build it. Prior-day levels use the regular session, 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern. Overnight levels run from 4 p.m. to the 9:30 open. The prior week runs Sunday 6 p.m. to Friday 4 p.m.
The 4 p.m. boundary matters. A high printed at 4:40 p.m. is not the prior day's high, however close to the close it was. It belongs to the overnight range.
Keep two saved chart templates, regular session and full session, both ending at 4 p.m.
The rule: only these six go on the list you mark before the session, each with its zone, far edge and session scope.
The in-session list. Some structure does not exist at 9:25 a.m. It forms in front of you, and the in-session list is just as fixed.
A level counts only once it has finished forming, and only if your plan named its type before 9:25. Before that moment it is a moving price, and the thing behind the stop has not finished happening.

The types are the opening range once your written window has closed, the defended pullback high or low, the developing VPOC and value edges at the price they show when your trigger fires, unfinished business, and the stacked imbalance as a location only.

Getting it wrong is using the opening-range high at 9:38 when your window runs to 9:45, or chasing a developing volume point of control as it slides with price. It will keep sliding, and you will keep chasing it. That is not a level. That is cardio.

segments.title: What is not a level
sections: Mid-Range, And The Lines That Are Not Levels

cues.text: Mid-range. It is the location tag for any price outside every zone on your list. It is not a kind of level. It is the absence of one.
It gets a name so a trade taken there is counted rather than hidden. Most of a chart, most of the time, is mid-range, and that asks nothing of you.

The lines that are not levels. Some lines look like levels and fail the test: VWAP, pivots, moving averages, Fibonacci lines, round numbers, fair value gaps, and chart patterns such as trendlines and triangles. They are popular. Popular is not the test.
Where one of these sits inside a real zone, the zone is the level. Where it sits outside every zone, the price is mid-range, whatever is drawn there.
A trade there is tagged mid-range, and it fails the first check of the grade rubric.
Locations and targets. A location is where a trade happens, with the stop behind the zone's far edge. A target is a level a trade aims at, written before entry. It is never a reason to enter.
The same level can be either. Its job in the trade is what changes.

On sessions that opened inside the prior session's value area, the prior session's VPOC was touched 82.4% of the time. That is TradingStats NQ app data, n=994 sessions. It is a touch rate measured from the open. It says nothing about direction or timing, and it is a target figure only.
Every trade at a level also records the test number: first touch of the zone that session, second, and so on.
The level you find afterwards. This part is about you, not the chart. Look at any chart after the close and levels are everywhere, because hindsight hands you the turn first and the reason second.
The rule: the list you mark before the session is closed at 9:25 a.m., and the in-session list adds only the types named on your plan. Nothing else becomes a level during the session.
At the end-of-day mark-up, count the lines you drew or noticed after 9:25 and write the number down.

It is an average that moves with price, so it never marks a place where something happened

check.q: The pd-vpoc zone is a location in one trade and a target in another. What changed?
options: The level's job in the trade

cues.text: The worked case. This is a composite chart. Every price is invented, and it stops at 9:25 a.m., before the open. There is no entry and no outcome.
8:50 a.m. Templates first: a regular-session template and a full-session template, both ending at 4 p.m. Eastern.
9 a.m. Collect the data by scope. From the regular session: high 24,186.50, low 24,032.00, value area high 24,148.00, low 24,071.00, volume point of control 24,112.00, settlement 24,131.50.
The overnight high is 24,190.00, printed at 4:12 p.m. It is above the regular-session high, but it came after 4 p.m., so it belongs to the overnight range. The prior-day high stays 24,186.50.
9:10. Write each level as a zone with its far edge. The prior-day high and overnight high zones overlap, so they become one row with the far edge at 24,190.00.
9:15. Everything outside those eleven rows is mid-range. Nothing is due there, which is the most relaxing sentence in this course.
9:18. Lines considered and not marked: the overnight VWAP, the round number at 24,100.00, a Fibonacci line, and a trendline. None passes the test.
9:20. Write the in-session line: which types you will watch, and each one's ready condition. The fifteen-minute opening-range window is this list's own choice, written once.
9:22. Targets go in their own column. The 9:25 list closes: eleven rows, one in-session line, one target column.
Notice where the time went. Not on finding more lines; the case struck four. It went on scope and edges.

Now score your own chart. One point for each true line: every row is a listed slug, every row has both edges and a side, every row has its stop sentence, every row names its scope, each slug has a written construction, the plan names its in-session types, and targets are marked apart.

Seven of seven: ready to plan from. Five or six: write the missing lines before 9:25. Under five: no trade at a level that session. A row that fails the zones line or the stop sentence line is struck for the day.

options: It becomes the on-high, and the pd-high stays 24,186.50
check.why: The print came after 16:00 ET, so it belongs to the overnight range. A template running to 17:00 ET would have misplaced it.

check.q: You score 5 or 6 on the "Does Your Chart Pass?" check. What do you do?

Take no trades at a level that session
Remove the lowest-scoring line and re-score
check.why: 7 of 7 means ready to plan from. Under 5 means no trade at a level that session.

check.q: You score under 5 on the chart check. What follows?
options: No trade at a level that session, and you mark the chart again tomorrow from blank
Half size at the strongest level
check.why: The score sets whether the chart can be planned from at all.

It is struck for the day, whatever the total
It moves to the target column
check.why: A row that fails line 2 or line 3 has no stop placement, so it is struck.

drill.title: Level-marking drill
drill.intro: Four synthetic charts. Every price and bar is invented; none comes from a real session. Two ask you to place the far edge of a zone. Two ask whether a line passes the stop-structure test. Nothing here is a trade, an entry or an outcome.

rounds.prompt: You are looking at a short from the high that price just turned at. Click the price of the far edge of that high's zone: the price your stop would sit behind.
rounds.why: The zone's far edge above price is the top, the extreme itself: 24,186.50. Six bars traded up into it and turned, and nothing traded above it, so a stop goes behind that price.

rounds.prompt: Now a long from the low that price just turned at. Click the price of the far edge of that low's zone.
rounds.why: Below price the far edge is the bottom, the extreme itself: 24,032.00. For a long, the stop goes behind that price. The reason for the trade is gone once price holds beyond it.

rounds.prompt: A line is drawn at 24,100.00. Does it pass the stop-structure test?
rounds.why: No. Price crossed the line again and again without turning at it. Nothing finished there, so there is no price beyond it at which a reason is gone. A stop behind it would be a number of points that felt right. It is mid-range.

rounds.prompt: A line is drawn at 24,161.00. Does it pass the stop-structure test?
rounds.why: Yes. Price traded up into 24,161.00 several times, turned each time, and nothing traded above it. Something already happened there, and a price beyond it gives a short a place for the stop. It passes.

cues.text: Your assignment. Before your next session's open, take one level from your chart and write it as one row.

The row holds the slug, its short name, then the near edge, far edge, side of price, session scope, and the stop sentence. One row. That is the whole assignment. It is small on purpose: one row you can defend is worth more than a chart full of lines you cannot.
The summary. A level is a zone of finished structure with a far edge a stop can sit behind, taken from a fixed list.
Everything else is mid-range, however it looks. And a level that price is expected to reach is a target, never a reason to enter.
Where it goes next. Module 07, Reading Order Flow, teaches the footprint read behind the stacked-imbalance location.
Modules 10 and 11 are the two reads at these zones. Module 13 is the trigger that must happen inside a zone before entry.
The level list is written each morning on the sheet in Module 16, and every branch of your plan in Module 15 names one of its zones.

check.q: What is the whole assignment in Before Your Next Session?
options: Mark every level on the chart again
Write one level as one row: slug, near edge, far edge, side of price, session scope and the stop sentence
check.why: One row. That's the whole assignment.

check.q: What goes in the journal's location field on every trade?
options: The slug, or mid-range, together with the test number
check.why: The test number records whether this was the first touch of the zone that session, the second, and so on.

check.q: Which module turns the far edge into a stop and the stop into a size?
check.why: Module 14, Trade Construction.

check.q: Which module sets two alerts on each zone, one at each edge?
check.why: Module 17, The Session And The Close.

questions.q: A line appears at 10:20 that was not on your plan. A trade at it is tagged how?
questions.why: The pre-marked list closes at 09:25, and the in-session list adds only the types named on the plan.

questions.q: The pd-high zone and the on-high zone overlap. How are they written?
options: As one row naming every slug in it, with the far edge at the outer edge
questions.why: If price is accepted above one but not the other, part of the structure is still standing.

questions.q: Which type of level is mostly a target rather than a location?
questions.why: A poor high is where a move already underway can reach, not a reason to start one.

questions.q: On this page, what is a stacked imbalance?
options: A location only, never a trigger
questions.why: Module 07 defines it and its settings.

questions.q: Which slugs have ETH, 16:00 ET to 09:30 ET, as their session scope?
questions.why: Overnight levels are built from ETH bars.

questions.q: A trade's stop was chosen after the entry as a number of points that "felt right". What does that reveal?
options: You chose where you wanted to trade, then looked for a reason, and the stop covered the gap
questions.why: The fix is a stop sentence on every row, written before the session.

questions.q: In the chain idea → setup → trigger → construction, where does the level sit?
options: Inside the setup's location, and it is where construction starts
questions.why: Get the level wrong and nothing after it can be built.

questions.q: The only level supporting an entry is in your target column. What do you do?
options: Don't take the entry, because it has no location
Move the level to the location column
questions.why: A target-column level is never the reason for an entry.
